title: Percent change
meaning: Percent change says how much a number grew or shrank, compared with where it started. A rise from 80 to 100 is a change of 20, and 20 is one quarter of the starting 80, so the change is 25%.
Analysts use it because a raw difference can mislead: going up by 20 is huge for a store that sold 10 last month and tiny for one that sold 10,000. Percent change puts both on the same scale.

formula.spoken: percent change equals new value minus old value, divided by old value, times 100

symbols.meaning: the starting value (the earlier period)
the ending value (the later period)
the change; it is negative when the value went down
turns a decimal such as 0.25 into a percent such as 25%

example.intro: A shop sold 80 mugs in May and 100 mugs in June. What is the percent change from May to June?

table.caption: Percent change from May to June, one step per row

Working
Result

steps: The old value is May (80), because May comes first.
The answer is positive, so it is an increase of 25%.

Check the other way: if sales fell from 100 back to 80, the change is −20 ÷ 100 = −0.20, a decrease of 20%. Going up 25% and then down 20% gets you back where you started, because each step divides by a different old value.

trap.wrong: Dividing by the new value: 20 ÷ 100 = 0.20, i.e. 20%.
trap.why: Percent change is always measured against where you started, so the old value goes on the bottom. Exam answer lists often include the divide-by-new result, so check which number you divided by before you pick.

title: Percentage points vs. percent
meaning: When the thing you are comparing is already a percent, such as a conversion rate, there are two ways to describe a change. Percentage points are the plain gap between the two percents; percent change is that gap compared with where you started.
Analysts must say which one they mean, because the same move can sound small (2 points) or large (50%), and readers make decisions on the number they hear.

formula.spoken: percentage point change equals the new percent minus the old percent

symbols.meaning: the starting rate, such as 4%
the ending rate, such as 6%
one unit on the percent scale; 4% to 6% is 2 points

example.intro: An email campaign's click rate went from 4% to 6%. Describe the change both ways.

table.caption: The same change as percentage points and as percent change
head: Measure
Working
Result

steps: Percentage points only subtract: no dividing.
Percent change uses the percent change rule from the previous lesson, with the old rate (4) on the bottom.
Both are true. "Up 2 points" and "up 50%" describe the same move.

trap.wrong: Saying the click rate "rose 2%" when it went from 4% to 6%.
trap.why: Going from 4% to 6% is 2 percentage points, but a 50% increase. "Rose 2%" would mean 4% became 4.08%. On the exam, read whether the question asks for points or percent.

title: Growth rates and ratios across periods
meaning: A period-over-period ratio divides one period's value by the one before it. A ratio above 1 means growth, below 1 means decline, and exactly 1 means no change.
Analysts use ratios to compare months, quarters or years quickly, and to see whether growth is steady.

formula.text: ratio = this period ÷ last period;  growth rate = (ratio − 1) × 100
formula.spoken: ratio equals this period divided by last period. Growth rate equals the ratio minus 1, times 100

symbols.meaning: the later value, such as February's sales
the earlier value, such as January's sales
the growth as a decimal; 1.10 − 1 = 0.10
turns the decimal into a percent

example.intro: A café served 100 customers in week 1, 110 in week 2 and 121 in week 3. Is growth steady?
steps: Each ratio is 1.10, so the café grows 10% every week.
The weekly gain in customers grows (10, then 11) even though the rate stays the same. That is compound growth.
This is the same as percent change: (110 − 100) ÷ 100 = 0.10.

trap.wrong: Reading a ratio of 0.8 as "80% growth".
trap.why: Subtract 1 first: 0.8 − 1 = −0.2, so the value fell 20%. Only the part above or below 1 is growth.

title: Compound annual growth rate (CAGR)
meaning: CAGR is the one steady yearly growth rate that would take a value from its start to its end over a number of years. It smooths out bumpy years into a single comparable rate.
Analysts use it to compare products or companies that grew over different spans, and because a simple average of yearly rates gives the wrong answer.

formula.spoken: CAGR equals end value divided by start value, raised to the power 1 over n, minus 1

symbols.meaning: the value at the beginning
the value at the finish
the number of years between start and end
the n-th root; with n = 2 it is the square root
leaves only the growth part; multiply by 100 for a percent

example.intro: Revenue grew from $100 to $144 (in thousands) over 2 years. What is the CAGR?

steps: Check: 100 × 1.2 = 120 after year 1, and 120 × 1.2 = 144 after year 2.
On a phone calculator, the n-th root is the same as raising to the power 1 ÷ n: 1.44 ^ 0.5 = 1.2.

trap.wrong: Averaging the yearly growth rates: +50% then −50% "averages to 0%".
trap.why: Each year's rate applies to a different starting value. 100 up 50% is 150, and 150 down 50% is 75, so the value fell. CAGR uses only the start, the end and n, which captures compounding.

title: Rule of 72
meaning: The Rule of 72 is a mental shortcut: divide 72 by a yearly growth rate to estimate how many years it takes a value to double.
Analysts use it to sanity-check growth claims without a calculator, such as whether "doubling in 3 years" is realistic.

formula.spoken: years to double is approximately 72 divided by the rate

symbols.meaning: the yearly growth rate written as a whole number, such as 6 for 6%
approximately; the rule is an estimate, not exact

example.intro: Users grow 6% per year. About how long until the user count doubles? And what rate doubles a value in 4 years?

table.caption: Using the Rule of 72 both ways
head: Question
Working
Result

steps: The rule works in either direction: 72 ÷ rate gives years, and 72 ÷ years gives the rate.
It assumes steady compound growth. It is closest for rates between about 5% and 10%.

trap.wrong: Writing the rate as a decimal: 72 ÷ 0.06 = 1,200 years.
trap.why: The rule is built for the whole-number percent. Use 72 ÷ 6, not 72 ÷ 0.06.

title: Weighted averages
meaning: A weighted average lets some values count more than others. Each value is multiplied by its weight (how many orders, credits or customers it stands for) before averaging.
Analysts need it whenever groups differ in size; a plain average of group averages treats a tiny group like a huge one.

formula.spoken: weighted average equals the sum of each weight times its value, divided by the sum of the weights

symbols.meaning: each value, such as a store's average order
each value's weight, such as that store's number of orders
the Greek letter sigma, meaning "add them all up"

example.intro: Team A has 3 people averaging 10 tickets a day; team B has 1 person averaging 30. What is the average per person across both teams?
steps: Divide Σ(w × x) by Σw: 60 ÷ 4 = 15 tickets per person.
The plain average of 10 and 30 is 20, which is too high because team B has only one person.

trap.why: That gives every group equal say no matter its size. Multiply each average by its count first, then divide by the total count.
